activity.overview: Show what you know about American expansion, the First World War and civil liberties at home, using the unit's sources.

problems.prompt: Which territories did the United States gain from the war with Spain in 1898? Give one reason Americans wanted them.
Quote the Anti-Imperialist League and explain its main objection, using one specific event from 1899-1902 as evidence.
Name one long-term cause and one triggering event of American entry into the First World War, and explain why each belongs in its category.
Why did Wilson describe the war's purpose as making the world "safe for democracy" rather than in terms of trade or territory?
Explain the "clear and present danger" test in your own words, and how the Court applied it to Schenck.

Debs said, "The master class has always declared the wars; the subject class has always fought the battles." Why did the government treat these words as a crime in 1918? Was it right to? Give one reason.
Why did the United States never join the League of Nations? Give two specific reasons.

activity.subject: history-social-studies
activity.title: Empire and War Unit Check

readings.body:
1898: The battleship Maine explodes in Havana harbor in February. In April the United States declares war on Spain over Cuba. The war lasts under four months. In the peace treaty Spain cedes Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States. Congress also annexes Hawaii.
1899: The Anti-Imperialist League opposes the annexation of the Philippines. Filipino forces who had fought Spain now fight the United States; the Philippine-American War lasts until 1902 and kills hundreds of thousands of Filipinos, most of them civilians.
1914: War breaks out in Europe in August. President Woodrow Wilson declares the United States neutral. American banks and businesses trade heavily with Britain and France.
1915: A German submarine sinks the British liner Lusitania in May; nearly 1,200 people die, 128 of them Americans. Germany later promises to limit submarine attacks.
1916: Wilson wins reelection; supporters use the slogan "He kept us out of war."
1917: In February Germany resumes unrestricted submarine warfare against all ships, including neutral ones. In March newspapers publish the Zimmermann Telegram, in which Germany's foreign minister proposed that Mexico join Germany in a war against the United States. On April 2 Wilson asks Congress to declare war; Congress declares war on April 6. In June Congress passes the Espionage Act.
1918: The Sedition Act expands the Espionage Act to punish criticism of the government and the war. More than two million American soldiers reach France. The fighting ends with the armistice of November 11.
1919-1920: Wilson helps write the Treaty of Versailles, which creates the League of Nations. The Senate twice refuses to ratify it, and the United States never joins the League.
readings.title: Empire and War, 1898-1920: A Timeline

readings.attribution: Platform of the American Anti-Imperialist League, October 1899. Public domain.
readings.body:
"We hold that the policy known as imperialism is hostile to liberty and tends toward militarism, an evil from which it has been our glory to be free."

About the source: The League's members included the industrialist Andrew Carnegie, the writer Mark Twain, the labor leader Samuel Gompers and former president Grover Cleveland. Supporters of annexation answered that the United States needed Pacific naval bases and markets in Asia, that rival empires would take the islands if the United States did not, and, in arguments shaped by the racial ideas of the time, that Filipinos were not ready to govern themselves.
readings.title: Platform of the American Anti-Imperialist League (1899), excerpt

readings.attribution: Woodrow Wilson, address to a joint session of Congress, April 2, 1917. Public domain (U.S. government work).
readings.body: "The world must be made safe for democracy. Its peace must be planted upon the tested foundations of political liberty."
readings.title: Woodrow Wilson, War Message to Congress (1917), excerpt

readings.attribution: Schenck v. United States, 249 U.S. 47 (1919), opinion of the Court by Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., March 3, 1919. Public domain (U.S. government work).
readings.body:
"The most stringent protection of free speech would not protect a man in falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic."

"The question in every case is whether the words used are used in such circumstances and are of such a nature as to create a clear and present danger that they will bring about the substantive evils that Congress has a right to prevent."

About the case: Charles Schenck, an official of the Socialist Party in Philadelphia, mailed leaflets urging men drafted into the army to oppose the draft. He was convicted under the Espionage Act, and the Supreme Court unanimously upheld his conviction. A week later the Court upheld Debs's conviction too.
readings.title: Schenck v. United States (1919), Justice Holmes for the Court, excerpts

readings.attribution: Eugene V. Debs, speech at Canton, Ohio, June 16, 1918. Public domain.
readings.body:
"The master class has always declared the wars; the subject class has always fought the battles."

About the source: Debs was the Socialist Party's candidate for president four times between 1900 and 1912. For this speech he was convicted under the Espionage Act, as amended in 1918, and sentenced to ten years in prison. In 1920 he ran for president from his prison cell and received more than 900,000 votes. President Warren Harding commuted his sentence in 1921.
readings.title: Eugene V. Debs, Speech at Canton, Ohio (1918), excerpt
